Derivations of Generalized Moduli Algebras of Isolated Hypersurface Singularities

Zhiwen Liu Address: Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications (BIMSA), Beijing, 100084, China Email address: liuzhiwen@bimsa.cn and Stephen S.-T. Yau Address: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing, 100084, China. Email address: yau@uic.edu
Abstract.

Let (V,0)(V,0) be an isolated complex hypersurface singularity defined by f∈ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn}f\in\mathbb{C}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}. Let A⁡(V)A(V) be the moduli(Tjurina) algebra, let A∗​(V)A^{*}(V) be the generalized moduli algebra, and let

L⁡(V)=Derℂ⁡(A⁡(V),A⁡(V)),L∗​(V)=Derℂ⁡(A∗​(V),A∗​(V))L(V)=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A(V),A(V)),\qquad L^{*}(V)=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A^{*}(V),A^{*}(V))

be the Yau algebra and the new Yau algebra of VV, respectively. Write λ⁡(V)=dimℂL⁡(V)\lambda(V)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}L(V) and λ∗​(V)=dimℂL∗​(V)\lambda^{*}(V)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}L^{*}(V). We prove that the difference between these two dimensions is determined by the Hessian corank. In the Morse case, the generalized moduli algebra is zero, and hence both derivation Lie algebras are zero. There is

λ∗​(V)=λ⁡(V)−{1,corank⁡Hess​(f)​(0)=1,0,corank⁡Hess​(f)​(0)≠1.\lambda^{*}(V)=\lambda(V)-\begin{cases}1,&\operatorname{corank}\operatorname{Hess}(f)(0)=1,\\ 0,&\operatorname{corank}\operatorname{Hess}(f)(0)\neq 1.\end{cases}

In particular, λ∗​(V)=λ​(V)\lambda^{*}(V)=\lambda(V) when n≥2n\geq 2 and mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3. This proves Conjecture 1.1 proposed in [3]. We construct an exact sequence whose two end terms are copies of the socle of the Milnor algebra. This homological approach reveals the detailed algebraic structure underlying the dimension count. We also give a alternative proof that pushes the original arguments in the proof of [3, Theorem C] further. The general case is obtained by combining Saito’s criterion for the non-quasi-homogeneous case.

Key words and phrases: 
isolated hypersurface singularity, moduli algebra, generalized moduli algebra, Yau algebra, derivation Lie algebra, Hessian determinant, socle, splitting lemma
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14B05; Secondary 13H10, 13N15, 32S05

1. Introduction

Let

𝒪n=ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn},𝔪=(x1,…,xn),\mathcal{O}_{n}=\mathbb{C}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\},\qquad\mathfrak{m}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}),

and let f∈𝔪2f\in\mathfrak{m}^{2} have an isolated critical point at the origin. Set (V,0)=V⁡(f)(V,0)=V(f) and write

Jf=(∂f∂x1,…,∂f∂xn),hf=detHess⁡(f),J_{f}=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}},\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}\right),\qquad h_{f}=\det\operatorname{Hess}(f),

where JfJ_{f} is the Jacobian ideal and hfh_{f} is the Hessian determinant. The quotient

A⁡(V)=𝒪n/(f,Jf)A(V)=\mathcal{O}_{n}/(f,J_{f})

is the moduli algebra, also known as the Tjurina algebra. The Mather–Yau theorem states that its isomorphism class determines and is determined by the analytic isomorphism type of the isolated hypersurface germ [10].

A key object of study is the derivation Lie algebra of A⁡(V)A(V),

L⁡(V)=Derℂ⁡(A⁡(V),A⁡(V)),L(V)=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A(V),A(V)),

which is a finite-dimensional Lie algebra. Yau proved that for any isolated hypersurface singularity, L⁡(V)L(V) is a solvable Lie algebra; see [14],[21]. This result led to L⁡(V)L(V) being named the Yau algebra [14, 22, 23], and

λ⁡(V)=dimℂL⁡(V)\lambda(V)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}L(V)

is its Yau number [7]. This establishes a profound connection between singularity theory and solvable Lie algebras.

In [3],the authors introduced the Artinian local algebra, i.e., the finite-dimensional quotient algebra

A∗​(V)=𝒪n/(f,Jf,hf)A^{*}(V)=\mathcal{O}_{n}/(f,J_{f},h_{f})

and called it the generalized moduli algebra [3]. The construction is motivated by Dimca’s theorem on zero-dimensional isolated complete intersections [5]: in the quasi-homogeneous case, the singular subspace of the Jacobian complete intersection has coordinate algebra A∗​(V)A^{*}(V). Together with the Mather–Yau theorem, this shows that A∗​(V)A^{*}(V) is a complete invariant within the quasi-homogeneous class; see [3, Remark 2.1]. The corresponding derivation Lie algebra and its dimension are

L∗​(V)=Derℂ⁡(A∗​(V),A∗​(V)),λ∗​(V)=dimℂL∗​(V).L^{*}(V)=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A^{*}(V),A^{*}(V)),\qquad\lambda^{*}(V)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}L^{*}(V).

We refer to L∗​(V)L^{*}(V) as the new Yau algebra. When A∗​(V)A^{*}(V) is the zero algebra, we use the convention Derℂ⁡(A∗​(V),A∗​(V))=0\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A^{*}(V),A^{*}(V))=0.

The construction of Yau algebras belongs to a broader interaction between singularity theory and finite-dimensional Lie theory. Brieskorn’s work relating rational double points to simple algebraic groups provides a classical instance of this interaction [16]. By the Levi decomposition, every finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra admits a decomposition

𝔤=𝔰⋉rad⁡(𝔤),\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{s}\ltimes\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak{g}),

where 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is a semisimple Levi subalgebra and rad⁡(𝔤)\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak{g}) is the solvable radical of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. The semisimple part admits a uniform classification in terms of root systems and Dynkin diagrams [17, 18], whereas solvable, and in particular nilpotent, Lie algebras do not admit a comparably uniform classification [19].

Yau’s construction provides a complementary geometric direction: it associates with every isolated hypersurface singularity a finite-dimensional solvable Lie algebra. It therefore gives a geometrically organized family of solvable Lie algebras that can be studied through local invariants of singularities; see also [14, 15, 20].

The new Yau algebra belongs to the same solvable Lie-theoretic framework throughout the range mult⁡(f)≥4\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 4. Indeed, if ff is not quasi-homogeneous, then A∗​(V)=A​(V)A^{*}(V)=A(V) and consequently L∗​(V)=L​(V)L^{*}(V)=L(V). If ff is quasi-homogeneous and mult⁡(f)≥4\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 4, it has been proved that L∗​(V)L^{*}(V) is solvable [3, Corollary 2.1]. Hence, for every isolated hypersurface singularity of multiplicity at least four, L⁡(V)L(V) and L∗​(V)L^{*}(V) are two finite-dimensional solvable Lie algebras naturally associated with the same singularity.

The comparison of their dimensions also has a direct geometric interpretation in terms of local algebras. For a finite-dimensional commutative ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra BB, the derivation algebra Derℂ⁡(B,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B) is the tangent Lie algebra at the identity of the algebraic automorphism group of BB; equivalently, it describes the infinitesimal algebra automorphisms of BB. Thus λ⁡(V)\lambda(V) and λ∗​(V)\lambda^{*}(V) measure the dimensions of the infinitesimal symmetry algebras encoded by the two intrinsic local algebras A⁡(V)A(V) and A∗​(V)A^{*}(V), respectively. Since

A∗​(V)=A⁡(V)/(hf¯),A^{*}(V)=A(V)/(\overline{h_{f}}),

determining the difference λ​(V)−λ∗​(V)\lambda(V)-\lambda^{*}(V) asks how imposing the additional Hessian relation changes the dimension of the infinitesimal symmetry algebra.

From both the Lie-theoretic and geometric viewpoints, it is therefore a natural and meaningful numerical problem. The following conjecture was proposed in [3].

Conjecture 1.1 ([3, Conjecture 1.1]).

Let n≥2n\geq 2, and let f∈𝒪nf\in\mathcal{O}_{n} define an isolated hypersurface singularity of multiplicity at least three. Then

(1.1) λ∗​(V)=λ​(V).\lambda^{*}(V)=\lambda(V).

The non-quasi-homogeneous case was already settled in the same paper. Indeed, Saito’s criterion gives hf∈(f,Jf)h_{f}\in(f,J_{f}), and hence A∗​(V)=A​(V)A^{*}(V)=A(V) [12, Corollary 3.8].

For weighted homogeneous singularities, the authors proved λ∗​(V)≤λ⁡(V)\lambda^{*}(V)\leq\lambda(V) in arbitrary dimension and equality when 2≤n≤42\leq n\leq 4. They also obtained equality for canonical weights

d≥2​w1≥2​w2≥⋯≥2​wn>0d\geq 2w_{1}\geq 2w_{2}\geq\cdots\geq 2w_{n}>0

under the additional condition wn≥w1/2w_{n}\geq w_{1}/2, and for binomial singularities; see [3, Theorems C and D, Remark 6.1, and Theorem 7.1].

Our first result proves 1.1 for weighted homogeneous singularities in every dimension, without an additional restriction on the weights. Combining this with the non-quasi-homogeneous case proves the conjecture in full. We then remove the multiplicity assumption and distinguish the two dimensions using Hessian corank.

Theorem A (Main theorem).

Let f∈𝔪2⊂𝒪nf\in\mathfrak{m}^{2}\subset\mathcal{O}_{n} define an isolated hypersurface singularity, and set

c⁡(f):=corank⁡Hess⁡(f)​(0)=dimℂker⁡Hess⁡(f)​(0),c(f):=\operatorname{corank}\operatorname{Hess}(f)(0)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker\operatorname{Hess}(f)(0),

where

Hess⁡(f)​(0)=(∂2f∂xi​∂xj​(0))1≤i,j≤n.\operatorname{Hess}(f)(0)=\left(\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{j}}(0)\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq n}.

Then the following statements hold.

  1. (1)

    If c⁡(f)=0c(f)=0, then ff is Morse,

    A⁡(V)≅ℂ,A∗​(V)=0,A(V)\cong\mathbb{C},\qquad A^{*}(V)=0,

    and

    λ⁡(V)=λ∗​(V)=0.\lambda(V)=\lambda^{*}(V)=0.
  2. (2)

    If c⁡(f)=1c(f)=1, then the Milnor number μ=μ⁡(V)\mu=\mu(V) satisfies μ≥2\mu\geq 2, and

    A⁡(V)≅ℂ⁡[t]/(tμ),A∗​(V)≅ℂ⁡[t]/(tμ−1).A(V)\cong\mathbb{C}[t]/(t^{\mu}),\qquad A^{*}(V)\cong\mathbb{C}[t]/(t^{\mu-1}).

    Hence

    λ⁡(V)=μ−1,λ∗​(V)=μ−2.\lambda(V)=\mu-1,\qquad\lambda^{*}(V)=\mu-2.
  3. (3)

    If c⁡(f)≥2c(f)\geq 2, then

    λ∗​(V)=λ​(V).\lambda^{*}(V)=\lambda(V).

We indicate the main steps of the proof. Suppose first that ff is a weighted homogeneous polynomial, n≥2n\geq 2, and mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3. The moduli algebra is then the Milnor algebra

Mf=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]/Jf,M_{f}=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]/J_{f},

and the class of hfh_{f} generates its one-dimensional socle. The adjugate-Hessian derivations and the relevant degree estimate appear already in the proof of [3, Theorem C]. Using relative derivations, we organize this calculation into the exact sequence of complex vector spaces

(1.2) 0⟶Soc⁡(Mf)⊕n\displaystyle 0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Soc}(M_{f})^{\oplus n} ⟶Derℂ⁡(Mf,Mf)\displaystyle\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M_{f},M_{f})
⟶Derℂ⁡(A∗​(V),A∗​(V))⟶Soc⁡(Mf)⊕n⟶0.\displaystyle\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A^{*}(V),A^{*}(V))\longrightarrow\operatorname{Soc}(M_{f})^{\oplus n}\longrightarrow 0.

The two end terms have the same dimension, giving the required dimension equality. We also record a shorter proof that combines the calculation in [3, Theorem C] with preservation of the socle under derivations.

Finally, the holomorphic splitting lemma [8, Theorem 2.47] reduces an arbitrary isolated hypersurface germ to a residual germ in c⁡(f)c(f) variables. The Morse case has no residual variables, one residual variable gives the corank-one exception, and a residual germ in at least two variables has multiplicity at least three. This proves the full corank formula.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 develops the local analytic background, the finite-dimensional algebras attached to a hypersurface germ, their derivation Lie algebras, and the required invariance facts. In Section 3 we review socles and treat the non-quasi-homogeneous case. In Section 4 we give the two proofs described above. In Section 5 we use the splitting lemma to prove A. Section 6 gives consequences and examples.

2. Preliminaries and invariance

2.1. Hypersurface germs and their local algebras

Let

Pn=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}P_{n}=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]}

be the polynomial ring in nn variables. The local analytic counterpart of PnP_{n} is the ring 𝒪n\mathcal{O}_{n} of germs of holomorphic functions at the origin of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. Recall that a germ records a holomorphic function only in an unspecified neighborhood of the origin: two functions represent the same germ when they agree on some smaller neighborhood. Taking Taylor series identifies

𝒪n=ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn},{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{O}_{n}=\mathbb{C}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\},}

the ring of convergent power series. It is a local ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra with maximal ideal

𝔪=(x1,…,xn)={g∈𝒪n:g⁡(0)=0}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathfrak{m}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=\{g\in\mathcal{O}_{n}:g(0)=0\}}

and residue field 𝒪n/𝔪≅ℂ\mathcal{O}_{n}/\mathfrak{m}\cong\mathbb{C}. A germ u∈𝒪nu\in\mathcal{O}_{n} is a unit precisely when u⁡(0)≠0u(0)\neq 0.

For f∈𝔪f\in\mathfrak{m}, the zero set of a representative of ff in a sufficiently small neighborhood of the origin defines a hypersurface germ, denoted by

(V,0)=V⁡(f)⊂(ℂn,0).{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}(V,0)=V(f)\subset(\mathbb{C}^{n},0).}

Only the behavior near the origin is retained. In particular, replacing ff by u​fuf, where uu is a unit, does not change the hypersurface germ. The local function algebra of VV is

F⁡(V)=𝒪n/(f),{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}F(V)=\mathcal{O}_{n}/(f),}

where (f)(f) is the principal ideal generated by ff. This algebra is usually infinite-dimensional over ℂ\mathbb{C}, but it is the natural local coordinate ring of the germ.

Throughout the paper, f∈𝔪2f\in\mathfrak{m}^{2}, so the origin is a critical point. The multiplicity of ff is

mult⁡(f)=max⁡{r≥1:f∈𝔪r};{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\operatorname{mult}(f)=\max\{r\geq 1:f\in\mathfrak{m}^{r}\};}

equivalently, it is the least total degree of a nonzero term in the power-series expansion of ff. Write

Jf=(∂f∂x1,…,∂f∂xn){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}J_{f}=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}},\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}\right)}

for the Jacobian ideal. We say that ff has an isolated critical point at the origin if, in a sufficiently small neighborhood, the gradient ∇f\nabla f vanishes only at the origin. Algebraically, this is equivalent to

Jf=𝔪,{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\sqrt{J_{f}}=\mathfrak{m},}

or, equivalently, to JfJ_{f} being 𝔪\mathfrak{m}-primary . Thus the quotient

Mf:=𝒪n/Jf{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}M_{f}:=\mathcal{O}_{n}/J_{f}}

is finite-dimensional. It is called the Milnor algebra of the defining germ ff. Whenever the defining germ is fixed, we also use the notation M⁡(V)=MfM(V)=M_{f}. Its dimension

μ⁡(V)=dimℂMf{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu(V)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}M_{f}}

is the Milnor number.

The Hessian matrix and its determinant are denoted by

Hess⁡(f)=(∂2f∂xi​∂xj)1≤i,j≤n,hf=detHess⁡(f).{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\operatorname{Hess}(f)=\left(\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{j}}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq n},\qquad h_{f}=\det\operatorname{Hess}(f).}

If f¯\overline{f} and h¯f\overline{h}_{f} are their classes in M⁡(V)M(V), then the moduli algebra can be written as

A⁡(V)=𝒪n/(f,Jf)=M⁡(V)/(f¯).{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}A(V)=\mathcal{O}_{n}/(f,J_{f})=M(V)/(\overline{f}).}

Thus A⁡(V)A(V) is its local coordinate algebra( also called the Tjurina algebra). The generalized moduli algebra is

A∗​(V)=𝒪n/(f,Jf,hf)=M⁡(V)/(f¯,h¯f),{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}A^{*}(V)=\mathcal{O}_{n}/(f,J_{f},h_{f})=M(V)/(\overline{f},\overline{h}_{f}),}

and is obtained by supposing the additional Hessian relation. Both are finite-dimensional quotients of the Milnor algebra. The number

τ⁡(V)=dimℂA⁡(V)\tau(V)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}A(V)

is the Tjurina number.The Mather–Yau theorem shows that the finite-dimensional algebra A⁡(V)A(V) determines and is determined by the analytic isomorphism type of the isolated hypersurface germ [10] . The role of A∗​(V)A^{*}(V) and the reason for adjoining the Hessian determinant are recalled below.

2.2. Weighted homogeneous singularities and the Hessian socle

Assign positive rational weights w1,…,wnw_{1},\ldots,w_{n} to the variables. The weighted degree of a monomial is

degw(x1a1⋯xnan)=∑i=1naiwi.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\deg_{w}(x_{1}^{a_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{a_{n}})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}w_{i}.}

A polynomial ff is weighted homogeneous, also called quasi-homogeneous, of weighted degree dd if every monomial occurring in ff has weighted degree dd. The tuple

(w1,…,wn,d){\color[rgb]{0,0,0}(w_{1},\ldots,w_{n};d)}

is its weight type. Multiplying all weights and dd by a common positive integer allows them to be taken integral. A hypersurface germ is called quasi-homogeneous if , after an analytic change of coordinates , it has a weighted homogeneous representative.

The weighted Euler vector field

E=∑i=1nwi​xi​∂∂xi{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}E=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}x_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}}

satisfies the Euler identity

E⁡(f)=∑i=1nwi​xi​∂f∂xi=d​f.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}E(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}x_{i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}=df.}

Consequently, f∈Jff\in J_{f} for a weighted homogeneous representative, and therefore

A⁡(V)=M⁡(V),τ⁡(V)=μ⁡(V).{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}A(V)=M(V),\qquad\tau(V)=\mu(V).}

The grading also gives

degw⁡(∂f∂xi)=d−wi,degw⁡(∂2f∂xi​∂xj)=d−wi−wj.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\deg_{w}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}\right)=d-w_{i},\qquad\deg_{w}\left(\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{j}}\right)=d-w_{i}-w_{j}.}

Every term in the Hessian determinant consequently has weighted degree

degw⁡(hf)=n​d−2​∑i=1nwi.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\deg_{w}(h_{f})=nd-2\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}.}

As explained below, this is the socle degree denoted by σ\sigma in Section 4.

For an isolated weighted homogeneous singularity, the Milnor number may also be read from the weights:

(2.1) μ⁡(V)=∏i=1nd−wiwi;{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mu(V)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{d-w_{i}}{w_{i}};}

indeed, the partial derivatives form a weighted homogeneous regular sequence of degrees d−w1,…,d−wnd-w_{1},\ldots,d-w_{n}, and the formula follows from the corresponding complete-intersection Hilbert series; see [3, Proposition 2.1] . When the weights are ordered and satisfy

d≥2​w1≥2​w2≥⋯≥2​wn>0,{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}d\geq 2w_{1}\geq 2w_{2}\geq\cdots\geq 2w_{n}>0,}

the weight type is called canonical.

We next recall the socle statement that links the Hessian determinant to the generalized moduli algebra. If (R,𝔫)(R,\mathfrak{n}) is a finite-dimensional local ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra, its socle is

Soc(R)=(0:R𝔫)={r∈R:𝔫r=0}.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\operatorname{Soc}(R)=(0:_{R}\mathfrak{n})=\{r\in R:\mathfrak{n}r=0\}.}

Thus the socle consists of the elements annihilated by the maximal ideal; if 𝔫s+1=0\mathfrak{n}^{s+1}=0 and 𝔫s≠0\mathfrak{n}^{s}\neq 0, then 𝔫s⊆Soc⁡(R)\mathfrak{n}^{s}\subseteq\operatorname{Soc}(R). Since JfJ_{f} is 𝔪\mathfrak{m}-primary and is generated by nn elements in the regular local ring 𝒪n\mathcal{O}_{n}, its generators form a regular sequence. Hence M⁡(V)M(V) is an Artinian complete intersection and, in particular, an Artinian Gorenstein algebra; see [2, Chapter 2] . A theorem of Scheja and Storch identifies its socle generator [13] :

(2.2) Soc⁡(M⁡(V))=ℂ​hf¯.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\operatorname{Soc}(M(V))=\mathbb{C}\overline{h_{f}}.}

In the quasi-homogeneous case , f∈Jff\in J_{f}, and it follows that

A∗​(V)=M⁡(V)/(h¯f)=M⁡(V)/Soc⁡(M⁡(V)).{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}A^{*}(V)=M(V)/(\overline{h}_{f})=M(V)/\operatorname{Soc}(M(V)).}

Consequently,

dimℂA∗​(V)=μ⁡(V)−1.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\dim_{\mathbb{C}}A^{*}(V)=\mu(V)-1.}

When μ⁡(V)=1\mu(V)=1, the Milnor algebra is ℂ\mathbb{C}, its socle is the whole algebra, and A∗​(V)A^{*}(V) is the zero algebra.

2.3. Derivations and the Yau algebras

Let RR be a commutative ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra and let NN be an RR-module. A ℂ\mathbb{C}-linear map D:R→ND:R\to N is a derivation if it satisfies the Leibniz rule

D⁡(a​b)=a​D​(b)+b​D​(a)D(ab)=aD(b)+bD(a)

for all a,b∈Ra,b\in R. In particular, D⁡(1)=0D(1)=0. We write Derℂ⁡(R,N)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(R,N) for the vector space of such maps . Equivalently,

Derℂ⁡(R,N)≅HomR⁡(ΩR/ℂ,N),\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(R,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(\Omega_{R/\mathbb{C}},N),

where ΩR/ℂ\Omega_{R/\mathbb{C}} is the module of Kähler differentials; see [6, Section 16.1].

For a concrete presentation, let P=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]P=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] and R=P/IR=P/I. A derivation D:R→ND:R\to N is determined by the elements

uj=D⁡(xj¯)∈N,1≤j≤n.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}u_{j}=D(\overline{x_{j}})\in N,\qquad 1\leq j\leq n.}

For every relation g∈Ig\in I, these elements must satisfy

0=D⁡(g¯)=∑j=1n∂g∂xj¯​uj.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}0=D(\overline{g})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\overline{\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_{j}}}\,u_{j}.}

Conversely, any tuple (u1,…,un)(u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}) satisfying these relations defines a derivation. In particular, when I=JfI=J_{f}, differentiating the relations ∂f/∂xi\partial f/\partial x_{i} produces the Hessian matrix. This is the presentation of relative derivations used in Section 4.

When N=RN=R, the commutator

[D1,D2]=D1​D2−D2​D1[{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}D_{1},D_{2}}]{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}=D_{1}D_{2}-D_{2}D_{1}}

is again a derivation. It therefore makes Derℂ⁡(R,R)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(R,R) a Lie algebra. If RR is finite-dimensional , then so is this Lie algebra. Moreover, an algebra isomorphism α:R→S\alpha:R\to S induces a Lie algebra isomorphism

Derℂ⁡(R,R)⟶Derℂ⁡(S,S),D⟼α​D​α−1.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(R,R)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(S,S),\qquad D\longmapsto\alpha D\alpha^{-1}.}

For the moduli algebra, this construction gives the Yau algebra

L⁡(V)=Derℂ⁡(A⁡(V),A⁡(V)),λ⁡(V)=dimℂL⁡(V).{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}L(V)=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A(V),A(V)),\qquad\lambda(V)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}L(V).}

Yau proved that L⁡(V)L(V) is solvable for every isolated hypersurface singularity [14, 15] . The corresponding objects for the generalized moduli algebra are the new Yau algebra and its dimension:

L∗​(V)=Derℂ⁡(A∗​(V),A∗​(V)),λ∗​(V)=dimℂL∗​(V).{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}L^{*}(V)=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A^{*}(V),A^{*}(V)),\qquad\lambda^{*}(V)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}L^{*}(V).}

When A∗​(V)A^{*}(V) is the zero algebra, we use the convention Derℂ⁡(0,0)=0\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(0,0)=0.

If I⊂RI\subset R is an ideal and π:R→R/I\pi:R\to R/I is the quotient map, composition with π\pi identifies

Derℂ⁡(R/I,R/I)≅{D∈Derℂ⁡(R,R/I):D⁡(I)=0}.\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(R/I,R/I)\cong\{D\in\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(R,R/I):D(I)=0\}.

Thus a derivation from RR to R/IR/I descends to the quotient precisely when it annihilates the defining ideal.

2.4. The generalized moduli algebra and contact invariance

The definition of A∗​(V)A^{*}(V) has a natural complete-intersection interpretation in the quasi-homogeneous case. The partial derivatives of ff define the zero-dimensional complete intersection

Xf=Spec⁡M⁡(V).{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}X_{f}=\operatorname{Spec}M(V).}

Its Jacobian matrix is the Hessian matrix of ff. Hence the singular subspace of XfX_{f} is defined by the Jacobian ideal together with the Hessian determinant, and its coordinate algebra is

𝒪n/(Jf,hf)=A∗​(V),{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{O}_{n}/(J_{f},h_{f})=A^{*}(V),}

where the last equality uses f∈Jff\in J_{f}. Dimca’s theorem states that a zero-dimensional isolated complete intersection is determined by its singular subspace [5] . Together with the Mather–Yau theorem, this gives the analytic invariance for A∗​(V)A^{*}(V) within the quasi-homogeneous class recorded in [3, Remark 2.1] .

Two germs f,g∈𝒪nf,g\in\mathcal{O}_{n} are right equivalent if g=f∘ϕg=f\circ\phi for an analytic coordinate change ϕ:(ℂn,0)→(ℂn,0)\phi:(\mathbb{C}^{n},0)\to(\mathbb{C}^{n},0). They are contact equivalent if

g=u⁡(f∘ϕ)g=u\,(f\circ\phi)

for some unit u∈𝒪n×u\in\mathcal{O}_{n}^{\times}.

For 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, let 𝔥k​(g)\mathfrak{h}_{k}(g) be the ideal generated by the k×kk\times k minors of Hess⁡(g)\operatorname{Hess}(g) and set

Hk​(g)=𝒪n/((g)+Jg+𝔥k​(g)).H_{k}(g)=\mathcal{O}_{n}/\bigl((g)+J_{g}+\mathfrak{h}_{k}(g)\bigr).

Dimca and Sticlaru proved that the isomorphism class of Hk​(g)H_{k}(g) is invariant under contact equivalence [4, Lemma 2.1]. Since 𝔥n​(g)=(hg)\mathfrak{h}_{n}(g)=(h_{g}), the generalized moduli algebra is the top local Hessian algebra:

A∗​(V⁡(g))=Hn​(g).A^{*}(V(g))=H_{n}(g).

We record this case explicitly because the transformation formula also proves the invariance of the Hessian corank used in A.

Proposition 2.1.

Let f,g∈𝔪2⊂𝒪nf,g\in\mathfrak{m}^{2}\subset\mathcal{O}_{n} define isolated hypersurface singularities. Assume that

g=u⁡(f∘ϕ),g=u\,(f\circ\phi),

where u∈𝒪n×u\in\mathcal{O}_{n}^{\times} and ϕ:(ℂn,0)→(ℂn,0)\phi:(\mathbb{C}^{n},0)\to(\mathbb{C}^{n},0) is an analytic coordinate change. Then

A⁡(V⁡(f))≅A⁡(V⁡(g)),A∗​(V⁡(f))≅A∗​(V⁡(g)).A(V(f))\cong A(V(g)),\qquad A^{*}(V(f))\cong A^{*}(V(g)).

Moreover,

corank⁡Hess⁡(f)​(0)=corank⁡Hess⁡(g)​(0).\operatorname{corank}\operatorname{Hess}(f)(0)=\operatorname{corank}\operatorname{Hess}(g)(0).
Proof.

We first consider g=f∘ϕg=f\circ\phi. Let JϕJ_{\phi} be the Jacobian matrix of ϕ\phi. The chain rule gives

∇g=Jϕt​(∇f)∘ϕ.\nabla g=J_{\phi}^{t}(\nabla f)\circ\phi.

Since JϕJ_{\phi} is invertible over 𝒪n\mathcal{O}_{n}, pullback by ϕ\phi identifies the Jacobian ideals. A second differentiation gives

(2.3) Hess⁡(g)=Jϕt​(Hess⁡(f)∘ϕ)​Jϕ+∑k=1n(fk∘ϕ)​Hess⁡(ϕk),\operatorname{Hess}(g)=J_{\phi}^{t}(\operatorname{Hess}(f)\circ\phi)J_{\phi}+\sum_{k=1}^{n}(f_{k}\circ\phi)\operatorname{Hess}(\phi_{k}),

where fk=∂f/∂xkf_{k}=\partial f/\partial x_{k}. The entries of the second term lie in JgJ_{g}. Taking determinants modulo JgJ_{g} gives

hg≡(detJϕ)2​(hf∘ϕ)(modJg).h_{g}\equiv(\det J_{\phi})^{2}(h_{f}\circ\phi)\pmod{J_{g}}.

The factor (detJϕ)2(\det J_{\phi})^{2} is a unit. This proves the two algebra isomorphisms under a coordinate change. Since ∇f​(0)=0\nabla f(0)=0, evaluation at the origin gives

Hess⁡(g)​(0)=Jϕ​(0)t​Hess⁡(f)​(0)​Jϕ​(0),\operatorname{Hess}(g)(0)=J_{\phi}(0)^{t}\operatorname{Hess}(f)(0)J_{\phi}(0),

so the corank is unchanged.

Now let g=u​fg=uf with uu a unit. The equality

∇g=u∇f+f∇u\nabla g=u\nabla f+f\nabla u

implies

(g,Jg)=(f,Jf).(g,J_{g})=(f,J_{f}).

Also,

(2.4) Hess⁡(g)=u​Hess⁡(f)+f​Hess⁡(u)+(∇u)​(∇f)t+(∇f)​(∇u)t.\operatorname{Hess}(g)=u\operatorname{Hess}(f)+f\operatorname{Hess}(u)+(\nabla u)(\nabla f)^{t}+(\nabla f)(\nabla u)^{t}.

Modulo (f,Jf)(f,J_{f}), this gives

hg≡un​hf.h_{g}\equiv u^{n}h_{f}.

Since unu^{n} is a unit, the generalized moduli algebras are isomorphic. At the origin,

Hess⁡(g)​(0)=u⁡(0)​Hess⁡(f)​(0),\operatorname{Hess}(g)(0)=u(0)\operatorname{Hess}(f)(0),

so the corank is again unchanged. ∎

The splitting lemma shows that the Hessian corank is exactly the number of residual variables left after the nondegenerate quadratic variables have been removed. This is why the statement of A is naturally organized by Hessian corank.

3. Socles and the non-quasi-homogeneous case

Let (R,𝔫)(R,\mathfrak{n}) be a finite-dimensional local ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra. The next two facts about its socle are standard. We include their short proofs because they are used at the central step of the argument. General background on Artinian Gorenstein rings and socles can be found in [2, Chapter 3].

Lemma 3.1.

Every nonzero ideal of RR meets Soc⁡(R)\operatorname{Soc}(R) nontrivially. If RR is Artinian Gorenstein, then every nonzero ideal contains Soc⁡(R)\operatorname{Soc}(R).

Proof.

Let I⊆RI\subseteq R be a nonzero ideal. Since RR is an Artinian local ring, its maximal ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m} is nilpotent. Thus, there exists a well-defined maximum integer r≥0r\geq 0 such that 𝔪r​I≠0\mathfrak{m}^{r}I\neq 0. By the maximality of rr, we have 𝔪r+1​I=0\mathfrak{m}^{r+1}I=0, which means 𝔪⁡(𝔪r​I)=0\mathfrak{m}(\mathfrak{m}^{r}I)=0. Consequently, the nonzero submodule 𝔪r​I\mathfrak{m}^{r}I is annihilated by 𝔪\mathfrak{m}, implying that 0≠𝔪r​I⊆Soc⁡(R)0\neq\mathfrak{m}^{r}I\subseteq\operatorname{Soc}(R). This proves the first assertion.

If RR is additionally Gorenstein, Soc⁡(R)\operatorname{Soc}(R) is a one-dimensional vector space over the residue field R/𝔪R/\mathfrak{m}. Since 𝔪r​I\mathfrak{m}^{r}I is a nonzero subspace of Soc⁡(R)\operatorname{Soc}(R), it must coincide with the entire socle. Hence, Soc⁡(R)=𝔪r​I⊆I\operatorname{Soc}(R)=\mathfrak{m}^{r}I\subseteq I, completing the proof. ∎

Lemma 3.2 (Socle preservation).

Let (R,𝔫)(R,\mathfrak{n}) be a finite-dimensional local ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra. Every D∈Derℂ⁡(R,R)D\in\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(R,R) satisfies

D⁡(𝔫)⊆𝔫,D⁡(Soc⁡(R))⊆Soc⁡(R).D(\mathfrak{n})\subseteq\mathfrak{n},\qquad D(\operatorname{Soc}(R))\subseteq\operatorname{Soc}(R).
Proof.

This is the local commutative case of Hochschild’s theorem that the radical of a finite-dimensional algebra over a field of characteristic zero is a characteristic ideal [9, Theorem 4.2]. We give a direct, self-contained proof.

Let us first show that D⁡(𝔫)⊆𝔫D(\mathfrak{n})\subseteq\mathfrak{n}. Since RR is a finite-dimensional local ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra, it is an Artinian local ring. Therefore, its unique maximal ideal 𝔫\mathfrak{n} coincides with its nilradical, which implies that every element a∈𝔫a\in\mathfrak{n} is nilpotent.

Let a∈𝔫a\in\mathfrak{n}, and suppose that D⁡(a)D(a) is a unit. Choose the least r≥1r\geq 1 with ar=0a^{r}=0. Since the characteristic is zero,

0=D⁡(ar)=r​ar−1​D​(a).0=D(a^{r})=ra^{r-1}D(a).

Cancelling the unit D⁡(a)D(a) gives ar−1=0a^{r-1}=0, a contradiction. Thus D⁡(a)∈𝔫D(a)\in\mathfrak{n}.

Now let s∈Soc⁡(R)s\in\operatorname{Soc}(R) and a∈𝔫a\in\mathfrak{n}. Since a​s=0as=0,

a​D​(s)=D⁡(a​s)−D⁡(a)​s=0.aD(s)=D(as)-D(a)s=0.

The last term is zero because D⁡(a)∈𝔫D(a)\in\mathfrak{n}. Hence D⁡(s)D(s) is annihilated by 𝔫\mathfrak{n} and lies in the socle. ∎

Proposition 3.3 (The non-quasi-homogeneous case).

If ff is not quasi-homogeneous, then

A∗​(V)=A​(V).A^{*}(V)=A(V).

Consequently,

L∗​(V)=L⁡(V),λ∗​(V)=λ⁡(V).L^{*}(V)=L(V),\qquad\lambda^{*}(V)=\lambda(V).
Proof.

This conclusion was already recorded in [3, p. 441], using [12, Corollary 3.8]. We give the equivalent socle argument.

By Saito’s criterion, f∈Jff\in J_{f} if and only if (V,0)(V,0) is quasi-homogeneous [11]. Thus f¯≠0\overline{f}\neq 0 in M⁡(V)M(V) in the present case. By lemma 3.1, the nonzero ideal (f¯)(\overline{f}) contains the one-dimensional socle of M⁡(V)M(V). In view of (2.2),

h¯f∈(f¯).\overline{h}_{f}\in(\overline{f}).

Therefore (f¯,h¯f)=(f¯)(\overline{f},\overline{h}_{f})=(\overline{f}) in M⁡(V)M(V), and the two quotient algebras are equal. ∎

4. The weighted homogeneous case

Throughout this section, let P=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]P=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], where n≥2n\geq 2, and let f∈Pf\in P be weighted homogeneous of degree dd with positive integer weights w1,…,wnw_{1},\ldots,w_{n}. Assume that the origin is an isolated critical point of ff and that mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3. The Jacobian ideal JfJ_{f} is then 𝔪\mathfrak{m}-primary, so P/JfP/J_{f} agrees naturally with the analytic Milnor algebra 𝒪n/Jf​𝒪n\mathcal{O}_{n}/J_{f}\mathcal{O}_{n}. Set

M=P/Jf,H=Hess⁡(f),h=detH,B=M/(h¯).M=P/J_{f},\qquad H=\operatorname{Hess}(f),\qquad h=\det H,\qquad B=M/(\overline{h}).

Euler’s identity and (2.2) identify these algebras as

M=A⁡(V),B=A∗​(V)=M/Soc⁡(M).M=A(V),\qquad B=A^{*}(V)=M/\operatorname{Soc}(M).

The partial derivatives of ff form a homogeneous regular sequence of degrees d−w1,…,d−wnd-w_{1},\ldots,d-w_{n}. Set

W=∑i=1nwi,σ=n​d−2​W.W=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i},\qquad\sigma=nd-2W.

The standard Hilbert-series formula for a graded complete intersection is

(4.1) HilbM⁡(t)=∏i=1n1−td−wi1−twi.\operatorname{Hilb}_{M}(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1-t^{d-w_{i}}}{1-t^{w_{i}}}.

It follows that

(4.2) Mq=0(q>σ),Mσ=ℂ​h¯,Bq=0(q≥σ).M_{q}=0\quad(q>\sigma),\qquad M_{\sigma}=\mathbb{C}\overline{h},\qquad B_{q}=0\quad(q\geq\sigma).

The adjugate-Hessian derivations and the degree estimate below occur already in the proof of [3, Theorem C]. Our purpose is to place that calculation in an exact sequence and then analyze the obstruction to descending a relative derivation to BB.

4.1. Relative derivations and the snake lemma

If NN is an MM-module, let Derℂ⁡(M,N)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,N) denote the space of ℂ\mathbb{C}-derivations from MM to NN.

Lemma 4.1.

There are natural identifications

Derℂ(M,M)≅ker(H:Mn→Mn),\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M)\cong\ker(H:M^{n}\to M^{n}),

and

Derℂ(M,B)≅ker(H:Bn→Bn).\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\cong\ker(H:B^{n}\to B^{n}).
Proof.

A derivation D:M→ND:M\to N is determined by

uj=D⁡(xj¯),1≤j≤n.u_{j}=D(\overline{x_{j}}),\qquad 1\leq j\leq n.

The relations fi=∂f/∂xi=0f_{i}=\partial f/\partial x_{i}=0 give

0=D⁡(fi¯)=∑j=1nfi​j¯​uj.0=D(\overline{f_{i}})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\overline{f_{ij}}u_{j}.

Thus the column vector (u1,…,un)t(u_{1},\ldots,u_{n})^{t} lies in the kernel of the Hessian matrix. Conversely, any vector in this kernel defines a derivation on the quotient. ∎

4.2. The Cramer derivations

We now compare the two kernels

ker(H:Mn→Mn)andker(H:Bn→Bn),\ker(H:M^{n}\to M^{n})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\ker(H:B^{n}\to B^{n}),

where

H=Hess⁡(f)H=\operatorname{Hess}(f)

is viewed as a matrix with entries in MM, and also as a matrix with entries in BB after reduction modulo (h¯)(\overline{h}).

By the result of Scheja and Storch [13],

Soc⁡(M)=ℂ​h¯.\operatorname{Soc}(M)=\mathbb{C}\overline{h}.

Set

Σ=Soc⁡(M)⊕n=(ℂ​h¯)⊕n⊂Mn.\Sigma=\operatorname{Soc}(M)^{\oplus n}=(\mathbb{C}\overline{h})^{\oplus n}\subset M^{n}.
Proposition 4.2.

There is an exact sequence of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces

(4.3) 0⟶Σ⟶Derℂ⁡(M,M)⟶Derℂ⁡(M,B)→∂Σ⟶0.0\longrightarrow\Sigma\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\xrightarrow{\partial}\Sigma\longrightarrow 0.

In particular,

dimℂDerℂ⁡(M,B)=dimℂDerℂ⁡(M,M).\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M).

Moreover, for p=1,…,np=1,\ldots,n, let Dp∈Derℂ⁡(M,B)D_{p}\in\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B) be the relative derivation defined by

(4.4) Dp​(xj¯)=π⁡(adj⁡(H)j​p¯),1≤j≤n,D_{p}(\overline{x_{j}})=\pi\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{adj}(H)_{jp}}\bigr),\qquad 1\leq j\leq n,

where π:M↠B\pi:M\twoheadrightarrow B is the quotient map. Then, with the usual convention for the connecting map,

(4.5) ∂(Dp)=h¯​ep,\partial(D_{p})=\overline{h}\,e_{p},

where epe_{p} is the pp-th standard basis vector of MnM^{n}. Hence the classes of

D1,…,DnD_{1},\ldots,D_{n}

span the quotient of Derℂ⁡(M,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B) by the image of Derℂ⁡(M,M)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M).

Proof.

We use the Hessian matrix

H=Hess⁡(f)H=\operatorname{Hess}(f)

as a matrix over MM, and also as a matrix over BB after reducing modulo (h¯)(\overline{h}). By lemma 4.1,

Derℂ(M,M)≅ker(H:Mn→Mn)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M)\cong\ker(H:M^{n}\to M^{n})

and

Derℂ(M,B)≅ker(H:Bn→Bn).\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\cong\ker(H:B^{n}\to B^{n}).

Under these identifications, the map

Derℂ⁡(M,M)⟶Derℂ⁡(M,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)

is induced by the quotient map

πn:Mn⟶Bn.\pi^{n}:M^{n}\longrightarrow B^{n}.

Since

B=M/(h¯)B=M/(\overline{h})

and

Soc⁡(M)=ℂ​h¯,\operatorname{Soc}(M)=\mathbb{C}\overline{h},

the kernel of πn\pi^{n} is exactly

Σ=(ℂ​h¯)⊕n.\Sigma=(\mathbb{C}\overline{h})^{\oplus n}.

Thus we have a short exact sequence

0⟶Σ⟶Mn→πnBn⟶0.0\longrightarrow\Sigma\longrightarrow M^{n}\xrightarrow{\pi^{n}}B^{n}\longrightarrow 0.

The multiplicity assumption is used at this point. Since mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3, every second partial derivative

fi​j=∂2f∂xi​∂xjf_{ij}=\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{j}}

has no constant term. Hence every entry of HH lies in the maximal ideal of MM. The maximal ideal kills the socle, so

H​Σ=0.H\Sigma=0.

Therefore HH gives a commutative diagram with exact rows:

The left vertical arrow is zero precisely because H​Σ=0H\Sigma=0.

Applying the snake lemma to this diagram gives an exact sequence

0⟶Σ\displaystyle 0\longrightarrow\Sigma ⟶ker(H:Mn→Mn)⟶ker(H:Bn→Bn)\displaystyle\longrightarrow\ker(H:M^{n}\to M^{n})\longrightarrow\ker(H:B^{n}\to B^{n})
→∂Σ⟶coker(H:Mn→Mn)⟶coker(H:Bn→Bn).\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\partial}\Sigma\longrightarrow\operatorname{coker}(H:M^{n}\to M^{n})\longrightarrow\operatorname{coker}(H:B^{n}\to B^{n}).

For completeness, the connecting map is as follows. Take

v¯∈ker(H:Bn→Bn)\overline{v}\in\ker(H:B^{n}\to B^{n})

and choose a lift

v∈Mn.v\in M^{n}.

Since H​v¯=0H\overline{v}=0 in BnB^{n}, we have

πn​(H​v)=0.\pi^{n}(Hv)=0.

Thus

H​v∈ker⁡(πn)=Σ.Hv\in\ker(\pi^{n})=\Sigma.

The connecting map is

∂(v¯)=H​v.\partial(\overline{v})=Hv.

This is independent of the choice of lift. Indeed, if v′v^{\prime} is another lift, then

v′−v∈Σ,v^{\prime}-v\in\Sigma,

and hence

H​adj⁡(H)=h​In.H\operatorname{adj}(H)=hI_{n}.

H​adj⁡(H)=h¯​In.H\operatorname{adj}(H)=\overline{h}\,I_{n}.

H⁡(adj⁡(H)​ep)=h¯​ep.H\bigl(\operatorname{adj}(H)e_{p}\bigr)=\overline{h}\,e_{p}.

The vectors

h¯​e1,…,h¯​en\overline{h}\,e_{1},\ldots,\overline{h}\,e_{n}

form a basis of Σ\Sigma. Hence

Σ⊆im(H:Mn→Mn).\Sigma\subseteq\operatorname{im}(H:M^{n}\to M^{n}).

Equivalently, the map

∂:ker(H:Bn→Bn)⟶Σ\partial:\ker(H:B^{n}\to B^{n})\longrightarrow\Sigma

0⟶Σ⟶ker(H:Mn→Mn)⟶ker(H:Bn→Bn)→∂Σ⟶0.0\longrightarrow\Sigma\longrightarrow\ker(H:M^{n}\to M^{n})\longrightarrow\ker(H:B^{n}\to B^{n})\xrightarrow{\partial}\Sigma\longrightarrow 0.

0⟶Σ⟶Derℂ⁡(M,M)⟶Derℂ⁡(M,B)→∂Σ⟶0.0\longrightarrow\Sigma\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\xrightarrow{\partial}\Sigma\longrightarrow 0.

H​π​(adj⁡(H)​ep)=π⁡(H​adj⁡(H)​ep)=π⁡(h¯​ep)=0H\,\pi(\operatorname{adj}(H)e_{p})=\pi(H\operatorname{adj}(H)e_{p})=\pi(\overline{h}\,e_{p})=0

in BnB^{n}. If we lift DpD_{p} to the vector

∂(Dp)=H​adj⁡(H)​ep=h¯​ep.\partial(D_{p})=H\operatorname{adj}(H)e_{p}=\overline{h}\,e_{p}.

Definition 4.3 (Cramer derivations).

The relative derivations

D1,…,Dn∈Derℂ⁡(M,B)D_{1},\ldots,D_{n}\in\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)

constructed in Proposition 4.2 are called the Cramer derivations, or adjugate-Hessian derivations. They are obtained from the columns of adj⁡(H)\operatorname{adj}(H) and satisfy

Dp(xj¯)=π(adj⁡(H)j​p¯),j=1,…,n,D_{p}(\overline{x_{j}})=\pi\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{adj}(H)_{jp}}\bigr),\qquad j=1,\ldots,n,

and

∂(Dp)=h¯​ep.\partial(D_{p})=\overline{h}\,e_{p}.

4.3. The descent obstruction

A relative derivation D:M→BD:M\to B descends to a derivation of BB if and only if it kills the kernel (h¯)(\overline{h}) of M↠BM\twoheadrightarrow B. Define

ob:Derℂ⁡(M,B)⟶B,ob⁡(D)=D⁡(h¯).\operatorname{ob}:\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\longrightarrow B,\qquad\operatorname{ob}(D)=D(\overline{h}).
Lemma 4.4.

The image of ob\operatorname{ob} is contained in Soc⁡(B)\operatorname{Soc}(B), and

(4.6) 0⟶Derℂ⁡(B,B)⟶Derℂ⁡(M,B)→obSoc⁡(B)0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ob}}\operatorname{Soc}(B)

is exact.

Proof.

Let a¯\overline{a} lie in the maximal ideal of MM. Since a¯​h¯=0\overline{a}\,\overline{h}=0 in MM, the Leibniz rule gives

0=D⁡(a¯​h¯)=π⁡(a¯)​D​(h¯)+π⁡(h¯)​D​(a¯)=π⁡(a¯)​D​(h¯),0=D(\overline{a}\,\overline{h})=\pi(\overline{a})D(\overline{h})+\pi(\overline{h})D(\overline{a})=\pi(\overline{a})D(\overline{h}),

Theorem 4.7.

Let f∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], n≥2n\geq 2, be weighted homogeneous with positive weights. Assume that ff has an isolated critical point at the origin and mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3. Let

M=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]/Jf,B=M/(h¯f).M=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]/J_{f},\qquad B=M/(\overline{h}_{f}).

(4.10) 0⟶Soc⁡(M)⊕n⟶Derℂ⁡(M,M)⟶Derℂ⁡(B,B)⟶Soc⁡(M)⊕n⟶0.0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Soc}(M)^{\oplus n}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Soc}(M)^{\oplus n}\longrightarrow 0.

dimℂDerℂ⁡(B,B)=dimℂDerℂ⁡(M,M).\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M).
Proof.

By Lemma 4.4, the natural map

Derℂ⁡(B,B)⟶Derℂ⁡(M,B),δ⟼δ∘π,\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B),\qquad\delta\longmapsto\delta\circ\pi,

identifies Derℂ⁡(B,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B) with

ker⁡(ob).\ker(\operatorname{ob}).

Derℂ⁡(B,B)≅Derℂ⁡(M,B).\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)\cong\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B).

Substituting this isomorphism into (4.3) gives (4.10). Taking dimensions yields

(4.11) dimℂDerℂ⁡(B,B)=dimℂDerℂ⁡(M,M).\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M).

∎

Remark 4.8.

The sequence (4.10) is an exact sequence of vector spaces. The middle map is a homomorphism of Lie algebras, but the entire sequence is not asserted to be exact in a category of Lie algebras.

4.5. An alternative proof

The previous proof of theorem 4.7 using the snake lemma provides a self-contained, exact-sequence reformulation of the adjugate calculation in [3]. We emphasize this homological approach because it reveals the complete algebraic structure underlying the dimension count. Specifically, the exact sequence (4.10) not only captures the dimension equality, but also explicitly explains why both the kernel and cokernel are exactly nn-dimensional, identifies the concrete derivation representatives for the cokernel, determines their precise grading degrees, and clarifies exactly how the mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3 assumption geometrically eliminates the descent obstruction to the socle quotient.

We now present a second, alternative proof that pushes the original arguments in the proof of [3, Theorem C] further. While it bypasses the rich structural information provided by the exact sequence, we record this direct approach.

Proposition 4.9.

Under the assumptions of theorem 4.7, one has

λ∗​(V)=λ​(V).\lambda^{*}(V)=\lambda(V).
Proof.

Use the notation

I=Jf,I′=I+(hf).I=J_{f},\qquad I^{\prime}=I+(h_{f}).

The proof of [3, Theorem C] considers the natural map

(4.12) φ:DerI′/I⁡(P/I)⟶Derℂ⁡(P/I′).\varphi:\operatorname{Der}_{I^{\prime}/I}(P/I)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(P/I^{\prime}).

Here DerI′/I⁡(P/I)\operatorname{Der}_{I^{\prime}/I}(P/I) denotes the derivations of P/IP/I that preserve the ideal I′/II^{\prime}/I. The kernel and cokernel calculations in that proof give

dimℂker⁡φ=n,dimℂcoker⁡φ=n.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker\varphi=n,\qquad\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{coker}\varphi=n.

The ideal I′/II^{\prime}/I is the one-dimensional socle of P/IP/I. By Lemma 3.2, every derivation of P/IP/I preserves this ideal. Hence

DerI′/I⁡(P/I)=Derℂ⁡(P/I).\operatorname{Der}_{I^{\prime}/I}(P/I)=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(P/I).

Taking dimensions in (4.12) gives

dimℂDerℂ⁡(P/I′)=dimℂDerℂ⁡(P/I).\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(P/I^{\prime})=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(P/I).

This is the desired equality. ∎

Theorem 4.10 (Conjecture 1.1 in [3]).

Let n≥2n\geq 2, and let f∈𝒪nf\in\mathcal{O}_{n} define an isolated hypersurface singularity with mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3. Then

λ∗​(V)=λ​(V).\lambda^{*}(V)=\lambda(V).
Proof.

If (V⁡(f),0)(V(f),0) is not quasi-homogeneous, apply Proposition 3.3. In the quasi-homogeneous case, choose a weighted homogeneous polynomial representative after an analytic change of coordinates. By Proposition 2.1, the moduli algebras, generalized moduli algebras, and their derivation Lie algebras are unchanged. The result now follows from theorem 4.7. ∎

5. Splitting and the Hessian corank

We now pass from the multiplicity statement to the full corank classification. The holomorphic splitting lemma, also called the generalized Morse lemma, states that a germ f∈𝔪2f\in\mathfrak{m}^{2} of Hessian corank cc is right equivalent to

(5.1) f∼rg⁡(x1,…,xc)+y12+⋯+yn−c2,f\stackrel{{\scriptstyle r}}{{\sim}}g(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c})+y_{1}^{2}+\cdots+y_{n-c}^{2},

where g∈(x1,…,xc)3g\in(x_{1},\ldots,x_{c})^{3} has an isolated critical point when c>0c>0 and is unique up to right equivalence [8, Theorem 2.47]. We first record the effect of the quadratic summands on the algebras in question.

Proposition 5.1.

Let g∈ℂ⁡{x1,…,xc}g\in\mathbb{C}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{c}\} have an isolated critical point, and set

F⁡(x,y)=g⁡(x)+y12+⋯+yr2.F(x,y)=g(x)+y_{1}^{2}+\cdots+y_{r}^{2}.

Then

A⁡(V⁡(F))≅A⁡(V⁡(g)),A∗​(V⁡(F))≅A∗​(V⁡(g)).A(V(F))\cong A(V(g)),\qquad A^{*}(V(F))\cong A^{*}(V(g)).

Consequently,

L⁡(V⁡(F))≅L⁡(V⁡(g)),L∗​(V⁡(F))≅L∗​(V⁡(g))L(V(F))\cong L(V(g)),\qquad L^{*}(V(F))\cong L^{*}(V(g))

as Lie algebras.

Proof.

The Jacobian ideal of FF is

JF=(Jg,y1,…,yr).J_{F}=(J_{g},y_{1},\ldots,y_{r}).

Thus all yiy_{i} vanish in the two quotient algebras. The Hessian matrix is block diagonal:

Hess⁡(F)=(Hess⁡(g)002​Ir).\operatorname{Hess}(F)=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Hess}(g)&0\\ 0&2I_{r}\end{pmatrix}.

Hence

hF=2r​hg.h_{F}=2^{r}h_{g}.

The algebra isomorphisms follow, and derivation Lie algebras are functorial under algebra isomorphisms. ∎

The standard classification of germs of corank at most one as type AkA_{k} is stated in [8, Theorem 2.48]. We include the short one-variable calculation because it also identifies the two Artinian algebras used here.

Lemma 5.2 (One residual variable).

Let g∈ℂ​{t}g\in\mathbb{C}\{t\} have an isolated critical point and order at least three. Then gg is right equivalent to tμ+1t^{\mu+1} for a unique integer μ≥2\mu\geq 2. Moreover,

A⁡(V⁡(g))≅ℂ⁡[t]/(tμ),A∗​(V⁡(g))≅ℂ⁡[t]/(tμ−1).A(V(g))\cong\mathbb{C}[t]/(t^{\mu}),\qquad A^{*}(V(g))\cong\mathbb{C}[t]/(t^{\mu-1}).
Proof.

Write

g⁡(t)=tμ+1​u​(t),u⁡(0)≠0.g(t)=t^{\mu+1}u(t),\qquad u(0)\neq 0.

An analytic (μ+1)(\mu+1)-st root of the unit uu gives a coordinate change that sends gg to tμ+1t^{\mu+1}. For this normal form,

g′​(t)=(μ+1)​tμ,g′′​(t)=μ⁡(μ+1)​tμ−1.g^{\prime}(t)=(\mu+1)t^{\mu},\qquad g^{\prime\prime}(t)=\mu(\mu+1)t^{\mu-1}.

The quotient presentations follow. ∎

Proof of A.

Apply the splitting lemma and Proposition 2.1, and then remove the quadratic variables by Proposition 5.1. It is enough to study the residual germ gg in c=c⁡(f)c=c(f) variables.

If c=0c=0, the holomorphic Morse lemma gives a nondegenerate quadratic form. Its moduli algebra is ℂ\mathbb{C}, while its Hessian determinant is a unit. Thus A∗​(V)=0A^{*}(V)=0, and both derivation spaces are zero.

If c=1c=1, apply Lemma 5.2. For N≥1N\geq 1, a derivation of ℂ⁡[t]/(tN)\mathbb{C}[t]/(t^{N}) is determined by an arbitrary element of (t)(t) as the value of tt. Hence

dimℂDerℂ⁡(ℂ⁡[t]/(tN))=N−1.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathbb{C}[t]/(t^{N}))=N-1.

This gives

λ⁡(V)=μ−1,λ∗​(V)=μ−2.\lambda(V)=\mu-1,\qquad\lambda^{*}(V)=\mu-2.

If c≥2c\geq 2, then the residual germ gg has multiplicity at least three in cc variables. Apply theorem 4.10. ∎

6. Consequences and examples

Corollary 6.1.

If n≥2n\geq 2 and mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3, then

λ∗​(V)=λ​(V).\lambda^{*}(V)=\lambda(V).
Proof.

The Hessian matrix vanishes at the origin, so c⁡(f)=n≥2c(f)=n\geq 2. Apply A. ∎

Corollary 6.2 (The corank-one exception).

Define

δH​(V)=λ⁡(V)−λ∗​(V).\delta_{H}(V)=\lambda(V)-\lambda^{*}(V).

Then δH​(V)∈{0,1}\delta_{H}(V)\in\{0,1\}, and δH​(V)=1\delta_{H}(V)=1 if and only if VV is stably right equivalent to an AkA_{k} singularity with k≥2k\geq 2.

Proof.

The splitting lemma reduces the corank-one case to one variable, where Lemma 5.2 gives the normal form tk+1t^{k+1}. The converse is immediate from the same normal form. The numerical statement follows from A. ∎

Corollary 6.3 (Plane curves and simple singularities).

For an isolated plane curve singularity, strict inequality λ∗​(V)<λ⁡(V)\lambda^{*}(V)<\lambda(V) occurs exactly for type AkA_{k}, k≥2k\geq 2. Among the simple hypersurface singularities, the same statement holds after adding or removing nondegenerate quadratic variables. In particular,

λ⁡(Ak)=k−1,λ∗​(Ak)=k−2,\lambda(A_{k})=k-1,\qquad\lambda^{*}(A_{k})=k-2,

while λ∗=λ\lambda^{*}=\lambda for Dk,E6,E7,E8D_{k},E_{6},E_{7},E_{8}.

Proof.

The standard normal forms are recalled in [1]. Type AkA_{k} has one residual variable. The residual forms of Dk,E6,E7,E8D_{k},E_{6},E_{7},E_{8} have two variables and order at least three. Apply A. ∎

Let k≥2k\geq 2 and

f=tk+1+y12+⋯+yr2.f=t^{k+1}+y_{1}^{2}+\cdots+y_{r}^{2}.

ei=ti​dd​t,1≤i≤k−1,e_{i}=t^{i}\frac{d}{dt},\qquad 1\leq i\leq k-1,

with bracket

[ei,ej]={(j−i)​ei+j−1,i+j−1≤k−1,0,i+j−1≥k.[e_{i},e_{j}]=\begin{cases}(j-i)e_{i+j-1},&i+j-1\leq k-1,\\ 0,&i+j-1\geq k.\end{cases}

The natural map L​(V)→L∗​(V)L(V)\to L^{*}(V) is surjective, and its kernel is ℂ​ek−1\mathbb{C}e_{k-1}. The one-dimensional defect is visible at the level of Lie algebras.

Example 6.5 (Multiplicity two with equality).

Consider

f=x3+y3+z12+⋯+zr2,r≥1.f=x^{3}+y^{3}+z_{1}^{2}+\cdots+z_{r}^{2},\qquad r\geq 1.

The multiplicity is two, but the Hessian corank is two. By quadratic suspension,

A⁡(V)≅ℂ⁡[x,y]/(x2,y2),A(V)\cong\mathbb{C}[x,y]/(x^{2},y^{2}),

and

A∗​(V)≅ℂ⁡[x,y]/(x2,x​y,y2).A^{*}(V)\cong\mathbb{C}[x,y]/(x^{2},xy,y^{2}).

x∂x,xy∂x,y∂y,xy∂y.x\partial_{x},\quad xy\partial_{x},\quad y\partial_{y},\quad xy\partial_{y}.

The second algebra has a square-zero maximal ideal of dimension two, so its derivation algebra is the full endomorphism algebra of that maximal ideal. Both dimensions are four. Thus multiplicity at least three is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one.

Example 6.6 (A multiplicity-two counterexample).

Let

f=xa​y+y2,a≥2.f=x^{a}y+y^{2},\qquad a\geq 2.

f=(y+12​xa)2−14​x2​a.f=\left(y+\frac{1}{2}x^{a}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}x^{2a}.

A⁡(V)≅ℂ⁡[x]/(x2​a−1),A∗​(V)≅ℂ⁡[x]/(x2​a−2),A(V)\cong\mathbb{C}[x]/(x^{2a-1}),\qquad A^{*}(V)\cong\mathbb{C}[x]/(x^{2a-2}),

and

A⁡(V⁡(f0))≅ℂ⁡[x,y]/(x2,y2),A(V(f_{0}))\cong\mathbb{C}[x,y]/(x^{2},y^{2}),

Appendix A Technical account of AIM-assisted exploratory work

This appendix records the role of the AI Mathematician (AIM) system described in [24] during the exploratory stage of this project. It does not add any hypothesis or result to the main text. All mathematical statements used in the paper were checked by the authors.

A.1. Starting point and responsibilities

The starting problem was to compare the Yau algebra and the new Yau algebra

L⁡(V)=Derℂ⁡(A⁡(V),A⁡(V)),L∗​(V)=Derℂ⁡(A∗​(V),A∗​(V)),L(V)=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A(V),A(V)),\qquad L^{*}(V)=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(A^{*}(V),A^{*}(V)),

and, in particular, to determine whether

λ∗​(V)=λ​(V).\lambda^{*}(V)=\lambda(V).

In the weighted homogeneous case, write M=A⁡(V)M=A(V) and B=A∗​(V)B=A^{*}(V). The authors proposed to compare Derℂ⁡(M,M)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M) and Derℂ⁡(B,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B) through the intermediate space Derℂ⁡(M,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B). The Hessian matrix describes Derℂ⁡(M,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B) as a kernel, while the gradient of the Hessian determinant gives the additional condition for an element of this space to define a derivation of BB. Exact sequences were then used to compare the three derivation spaces. AIM was used to organize possible steps in this approach, test examples, and examine candidate intermediate statements.

The AIM output was treated as exploratory material, not as a proof. The authors were responsible for the final theorem and its proof. They verified every argument included in the paper. The authors take responsibility for all statements and proofs.

A.2. The weighted homogeneous case

Let f∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], n≥2n\geq 2, be weighted homogeneous with an isolated critical point, and assume that mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3. Set

M=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]/Jf,H=Hess⁡(f),h=detH,B=M/(h¯).M=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]/J_{f},\qquad H=\operatorname{Hess}(f),\qquad h=\det H,\qquad B=M/(\overline{h}).

Euler’s identity and the classical theorem in [13] give

M=A⁡(V),Soc⁡(M)=ℂ​h¯,B=A∗​(V)=M/Soc⁡(M).M=A(V),\qquad\operatorname{Soc}(M)=\mathbb{C}\overline{h},\qquad B=A^{*}(V)=M/\operatorname{Soc}(M).

If ff has weighted degree dd, the variables have positive weights w1,…,wnw_{1},\ldots,w_{n}, and W=∑iwiW=\sum_{i}w_{i}, then

HilbM⁡(t)=∏i=1n1−td−wi1−twi,σ=n​d−2​W.\operatorname{Hilb}_{M}(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1-t^{d-w_{i}}}{1-t^{w_{i}}},\qquad\sigma=nd-2W.

In particular,

Mσ=ℂh¯,Bq=0(q≥σ),dimℂB=μ(V)−1.M_{\sigma}=\mathbb{C}\overline{h},\qquad B_{q}=0\quad(q\geq\sigma),\qquad\dim_{\mathbb{C}}B=\mu(V)-1.

These are standard facts and were used as inputs to the exploration.

The relations defining derivations give

Derℂ(M,B)≅ker(H:Bn⟶Bn)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\cong\ker\bigl(H:B^{n}\longrightarrow B^{n}\bigr)

and

Derℂ(B,B)≅ker([H∇h¯t]:Bn⟶Bn+1).\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)\cong\ker\left(\begin{bmatrix}H\\ \overline{\nabla h}^{\,t}\end{bmatrix}:B^{n}\longrightarrow B^{n+1}\right).

Under these identifications, a derivation D:M→BD:M\to B induces a derivation of B=M/(h¯)B=M/(\overline{h}) precisely when it vanishes on

(h¯)=ker⁡(M⟶B),(\overline{h})=\ker(M\longrightarrow B),

or equivalently when D⁡(h¯)=0D(\overline{h})=0. This condition is measured by

ob:ker(H:Bn⟶Bn)⟶B,u⟼∇h¯tu.\operatorname{ob}:\ker\bigl(H:B^{n}\longrightarrow B^{n}\bigr)\longrightarrow B,\qquad u\longmapsto\overline{\nabla h}^{\,t}u.

Equivalently, if uu represents D∈Derℂ⁡(M,B)D\in\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B), then

ob⁡(D)=D⁡(h¯).\operatorname{ob}(D)=D(\overline{h}).

It follows that

dimℂDerℂ⁡(M,B)−dimℂDerℂ⁡(B,B)=rankℂ⁡(ob).\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)-\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{C}}(\operatorname{ob}).

This converts the dimension comparison into a question about one specified map.

A.3. Exact sequence and Cramer derivations

The authors proposed to compare Derℂ⁡(M,M)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M) and Derℂ⁡(B,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B) through the intermediate space Derℂ⁡(M,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B). A pre-manuscript note generated with AIM developed this proposal into a preliminary two-step argument for the weighted homogeneous case.

The adjugate-Hessian derivations and the degree estimate used in this argument already appear in [3, Theorem C]. The AIM-generated note did not originate these ingredients. It used them in the comparison of the three derivation spaces described above.

The first step compares Derℂ⁡(M,M)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M) with Derℂ⁡(M,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B). Since

B=M/(h¯),Soc⁡(M)=ℂ​h¯,B=M/(\overline{h}),\qquad\operatorname{Soc}(M)=\mathbb{C}\overline{h},

the quotient map Mn→BnM^{n}\to B^{n} gives a short exact sequence

0⟶Soc⁡(M)⊕n⟶Mn⟶Bn⟶0.0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Soc}(M)^{\oplus n}\longrightarrow M^{n}\longrightarrow B^{n}\longrightarrow 0.

The Hessian matrix acts on both MnM^{n} and BnB^{n}. Since mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3, its entries lie in the maximal ideal of MM, and hence

H​Soc⁡(M)⊕n=0.H\operatorname{Soc}(M)^{\oplus n}=0.

Therefore there is a commutative diagram with exact rows:

Applying the snake lemma to this diagram, and then using H​adj⁡(H)=h​InH\operatorname{adj}(H)=hI_{n} gives the exact sequence

0⟶Soc⁡(M)⊕n⟶Derℂ⁡(M,M)⟶Derℂ⁡(M,B)→∂Soc⁡(M)⊕n⟶0.0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Soc}(M)^{\oplus n}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\xrightarrow{\partial}\operatorname{Soc}(M)^{\oplus n}\longrightarrow 0.

Consequently,

dimℂDerℂ⁡(M,B)=dimℂDerℂ⁡(M,M).\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M).

For p=1,…,np=1,\ldots,n, the pp-th column of adj⁡(H)\operatorname{adj}(H) defines a derivation Dp:M→BD_{p}:M\to B by

Dp​(xj¯)=π⁡(adj⁡(H)j​p¯),1≤j≤n,D_{p}(\overline{x_{j}})=\pi\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{adj}(H)_{jp}}\bigr),\qquad 1\leq j\leq n,

where π:M→B\pi:M\to B is the quotient map. Cramer’s identity gives

∂(Dp)=h¯​ep.\partial(D_{p})=\overline{h}\,e_{p}.

The classes of D1,…,DnD_{1},\ldots,D_{n} therefore span the quotient

Q:=Derℂ⁡(M,B)/im⁡(Derℂ⁡(M,M)⟶Derℂ⁡(M,B)).Q:=\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\big/\operatorname{im}\bigl(\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\bigr).

The second step determines which derivations D:M→BD:M\to B define derivations of the quotient algebra B=M/(h¯)B=M/(\overline{h}). Such a derivation defines a derivation of BB precisely when

D⁡(h¯)=0.D(\overline{h})=0.

The AIM-generated note organized this condition through the map

ob:Derℂ⁡(M,B)⟶B,ob⁡(D)=D⁡(h¯).\operatorname{ob}:\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B)\longrightarrow B,\qquad\operatorname{ob}(D)=D(\overline{h}).

Preservation of the one-dimensional socle of MM shows that ob\operatorname{ob} vanishes on the image of Derℂ⁡(M,M)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M). For the derivations DpD_{p}, one has

deg⁡(Dp)=ϵp=σ−d+wp.\deg(D_{p})=\epsilon_{p}=\sigma-d+w_{p}.

The degree estimate gives ϵp≥0\epsilon_{p}\geq 0. Since h¯\overline{h} has degree σ\sigma and

Bq=0(q≥σ),B_{q}=0\qquad(q\geq\sigma),

it follows that

ob⁡(Dp)=Dp​(h¯)∈Bσ+ϵp=0.\operatorname{ob}(D_{p})=D_{p}(\overline{h})\in B_{\sigma+\epsilon_{p}}=0.

The classes of the DpD_{p} span QQ. Hence ob=0\operatorname{ob}=0 on all of Derℂ⁡(M,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B). Every derivation M→BM\to B therefore defines a derivation of BB, and

dimℂDerℂ⁡(B,B)=dimℂDerℂ⁡(M,B).\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B).

Together with the first step, this gives

dimℂDerℂ⁡(B,B)=dimℂDerℂ⁡(M,M).\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M).

The AIM-generated note contained this preliminary two-step argument. The authors checked every map, degree calculation, and exactness statement, corrected the intermediate argument where necessary, and wrote the final proof given in the manuscript.

A.4. AIM-assisted examples

AIM was used to explore and check examples that were later included in the final section of the paper. For the AkA_{k} singularities, the calculation shows that the natural map

L​(V)⟶L∗​(V)L(V)\longrightarrow L^{*}(V)

has a one-dimensional kernel. AIM-assisted calculations also gave

λ⁡(V)=λ∗​(V)=4\lambda(V)=\lambda^{*}(V)=4

for f=x3+y3+∑zi2f=x^{3}+y^{3}+\sum z_{i}^{2}, and a difference of one for f=xa​y+y2f=x^{a}y+y^{2}. For the family

fs=x3+y3+s​x​y+z2,f_{s}=x^{3}+y^{3}+sxy+z^{2},

both dimensions are zero for s≠0s\neq 0, whereas for s=0s=0, both dimensions are four. Thus their common value may jump even though the equality between them is preserved.

The authors selected the examples, verified all calculations, and included them to illustrate the main result.

A.5. Scope of assistance

The main purpose of the paper is to prove

λ∗​(V)=λ​(V)\lambda^{*}(V)=\lambda(V)

for isolated hypersurface singularities with n≥2n\geq 2 and mult⁡(f)≥3\operatorname{mult}(f)\geq 3, thereby proving Conjecture 1.1. The authors formulated the problem and proposed comparing Derℂ⁡(M,M)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,M) and Derℂ⁡(B,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(B,B) through Derℂ⁡(M,B)\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{C}}(M,B). A pre-manuscript note generated with AIM contained a preliminary two-step argument for the weighted homogeneous case. AIM was also used for preliminary calculations of the examples.

The adjugate-Hessian derivations and the required degree estimate were already known from earlier work and are not attributed to AIM. The authors checked and corrected the preliminary argument, supplied the remaining arguments needed to prove the conjecture in full, and wrote the final proof. They take responsibility for every mathematical statement and calculation in the paper.

A.6. Internal development record

This account is based on dated AIM session records from June 2026 and an AIM workspace note dated 5 July 2026, both of which precede the manuscript version dated 29 July 2026. These materials record when the exploratory calculations and the exact-sequence organization described above were written down. Because the records are not publicly available, readers cannot use them to verify the origin of individual arguments.
